title: Surgical Incisions in Low-Resource Settings
subject: Surgery
summary: Surgical incisions are deliberate skin cuts that expose operative fields. In low-resource hospitals, technique, choice of suture, and infection control are critical. Clinicians must assess incision integrity, anticipate complications, and manage with limited diagnostics.

sections.p: A surgical incision is a planned cut through skin and subcutaneous tissue to access deeper structures. Diagnosis is clinical: location, size, and appearance of the wound.
b: Plan the incision based on anatomy and pathology

sections.p: Incisions are staged by depth and contamination: superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness, clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated, dirty.
b: Full-thickness clean incisions have lowest infection risk

sections.p: Incisions are intentional; complications arise from poor technique, infection, or patient factors such as malnutrition, HIV, or diabetes.
b: HIV and TB increase infection risk

sections.p: Incisions appear as linear wounds with edges that may be approximated or sutured. Signs of poor healing include dehiscence, excessive drainage, or erythema.
Limited investigations are available; focus on clinical assessment and basic labs.

Anemia reduces oxygen delivery to the wound
Identifies bacterial flora; guides antibiotic choice

sections.p: Complications include infection, dehiscence, hematoma, and poor cosmetic outcome. Red flags: fever, purulent drainage, pain out of proportion, or wound separation.
Manage by ensuring aseptic technique, appropriate suture material, and postoperative care. Antibiotics are reserved for infected wounds.
b: Administer prophylactic antibiotics only if contamination is high

t.b: Use first‑generation cephalosporin if available; avoid penicillin in penicillin‑allergic patients; consider clindamycin if MRSA risk is high

sections.p: Follow-up focuses on wound inspection, pain control, and early mobilization. Prevention includes preoperative skin prep, hand hygiene, and patient education.
b: Encourage early ambulation to prevent venous stasis

sections.p: Incision infection can mimic cellulitis; dehiscence may be mistaken for poor surgical technique.
b: Dehiscence: visible separation of wound edges

sections.p: Normal white cell count may mask infection in immunocompromised patients; low CRP can occur in early infection.
b: CRP may be low in early postoperative period

faq.q: What is the best suture material for skin in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: A non‑absorbable nylon or polypropylene is preferred for skin; absorbable sutures are used for subcutaneous layers.

faq.q: When should I give antibiotics after a clean incision?
faq.a: Only if the incision is contaminated or the patient has risk factors like diabetes or HIV; otherwise, prophylaxis is not needed.

faq.q: How do I recognise a wound infection early?
faq.a: Look for erythema, warmth, swelling, pain, purulent drainage, or fever within the first 48–72 hours post‑op.

exam: What is the first step in managing a dehisced incision? — Inspect for infection, re‑approximate edges, and consider antibiotics if contaminated.
Which suture material is least likely to cause allergic reaction in skin closure? — Non‑absorbable nylon or polypropylene.
Why is a clean‑contaminated incision more likely to develop infection than a clean incision? — Presence of normal flora from the surgical field increases bacterial load.
What is the most common bacterial cause of postoperative wound infection in East Africa? — Staphylococcus aureus, often methicillin‑resistant.
When should you avoid using a first‑generation cephalosporin for prophylaxis? — In patients with a known penicillin allergy or high MRSA prevalence.
How do you differentiate cellulitis from incision infection? — Cellulitis spreads beyond incision margins; incision infection is confined to the wound edges.
What is the key sign of a hematoma at a surgical site? — Swelling, bruising, and pain that worsens with movement.
Which laboratory test is most useful when a wound culture is unavailable? — White cell count and CRP to gauge systemic inflammation.
